Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 1, 2024
Review Body:
This could have been a fine book, but it's very transparently just propaganda written in the hopes of either a) convincing people not to vote Trump in 2024, or b) making money by selling copies to folks on the left who want to be told they're correct. I had hoped it would be more, but alas.

The format for each chapter was very simple: here is an example from history, here is the principle I'd like you to extract from it, and then the author seemed to flip a coin regarding whether he'd give an example of how Trump violated that principle. His allusions to "an American president/presidential candidate" would have been perhaps less of an eye-roll if he had ever cited violations of principle from the other side of the aisle - performatively feigned journalistic objectivity is just tiresome.

I really wanted to like this book - the principles espoused aren't wrong. If it had examined both parties, and had fleshed out the ideas to help the reader broaden their perspective (which was why I bought the book), it could have been a fine book. But alas, the author clearly just wanted to shout "Trump represents tyranny, here is how to fight him" while giving some historical anecdotes to give a veneer of insight. Definitely don't buy it, and if you come across it at a library, it may not even be worth the time you spend to read it - there's nothing insightful here.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on February 7, 2022
Review Body:
The good:

1.References from history were good. I do only know that because I had already read them in other sources.

2. Some of the broader theses posited at the beginnings of chapters elicit some interesting possibilities for debate.

The bad (only some because there is a lot):

1. Sources are virtually nonexistent in this book. When you make incredible claims, you require incredible soucing. The best we typically get is the name of 1 of the 5 or so authors/historians/philosophers he relies on throughout without so much as the work he is pulling that from.
This lack of academic rigor plagues this book.

2. Passivity of voice. The prose itself is weak. He refers to Trump throughout but never by name. It reads like a teenage girl's diary speaking of a former lover.
This despite using numerous examples that have long been debunked. I will give him the benefit of the doubt and assume he wrote these prior to the stories having doubt cast upon them, but given the brevity and pop-academia nature of the book, it surely took no longer than a weekend to write.
This damages his anti-Trump arguments that do have some legs e.g. calling any reporter "fake news" who merely disagrees with him. It only leads you to want to doubt all of his arguments. Arguments which are conclusory at best.

3. Willfully ignoring counterarguments that damage "his side" of the debate. Related to the second point of the good above, he often posits a thesis, ignores times the thesis is more indicative of the American Left than it is Trump/the Right.
He compounds the issue by making no attempt to distinguish why the violations of his presupposes norms by Trump/the Right matter and the Left's do not.
The glaring example was his claim that doubting elections was an damnable offense and only notes Trump's weakly supported protestations of the 2020 election.
2000- Gore challenged the results
2004- Democrats preemptively insinuated, with the help of the media, that Bush owned Diebold voting machines and was rigging them.
2008- Democrats, with the help of the media, push the idea that the new KKK was going to stop people from voting Obama. This spurred leftist militant groups patrolling polling places. The most notable was a Black Panther cell engaging in voter intimidation in Philadelphia-- then given a walk by the DOJ once the election was over.
2012- Democrats stick with the trope that Romney was going to put "y'all back in chains" referring to black people.
2016- Russiagate. The Mueller report dismissed that outright as a weak attempt to purchase facebook ads and forming astroturf facebook events that resulted in audiences of fewer than 10 people. The report focused mostly on potential obstruction of justice pertaining to the investigation of the dead end claim.
2020- Biden/Harris, citing the debunked Russiagate, preemptively claim Russians were going to rig 2020 "like they did 2016" despite a $50million dollar investigation saying otherwise.
This is only the examples of presidential years. Things like Stacey Abrams still referring to herself as the true governor of Georgia 4 years hence are also worthy examples.

If you want to take Trump to task for doubting 2020 based on thin evidence, that is fair. When you ignore the much broader pattern of the Left casting doubts on elections, you ignore a giant hole in the premise. He notes in his historical examples that Left and Right have ushered in tyranny in Europe. This book would make you think that a Left driven tyranny in the US is not possible in any sense. A preposterous idea to be sure.

Conclusion:
There are a litany of other issues but the point is made. This book had a chance to truly dissect the tyrannical tendencies of the Left and Right. Instead it has the same level of objectivity of a Sean Hannity interview of Donald Trump.

If you are a "default liberal" who believes democrats do nothing wrong, you'll ignore the obvious flaws and find this a prescient work.
Full on "Trump does no wrong" crowd will hate it for any critique of Trump (which is a separate issue).
Independents, non-democrat leftists, and those on the Right not closely Trump aligned will find this book riddled with sophistry and lacking any intellectual discourse at all.
If you want some aphorisms of historical events from 1920-1991 Europe, and that's all you want, you may enjoy this a bit.

The only reason I give it 2 stars is that it only takes 40 minutes or so to read and it's good to know what a pseudointellectual exercise dressed up in credentialism looks like; so you can identify and avoid it in the future.

The Obama administration had its share of tyrannical overreaches that would fit nicely in this slim volume, but not once were any of them even hinted at. I was curious to see if Snyder would later apply ANY of his lessons to the current Biden administration (the book was published in 2017), but after spending several minutes looking through his recent articles and Twitter feed, he not only neglects to be consistent from one administration to the next, but he is clearly a shill for the democratic party. I am no fan of Donald Trump, but the radicalism of the progressive left is far more concerning, and the policies and rhetoric of the current administration (as opposed to just the rhetoric of the past) are often textbook examples of what Snyder attempts to expose in this book. It is fascinating that Snyder's own work beyond "On Tyranny" actually appears to ignore many of the lessons he sets forth that, without the obvious bias, are true and helpful. If you are good at eating meat and discarding bones, there are good things to take away from this book. Otherwise, you're better off looking elsewhere.

We are also told that Trump is dangerous because he criticized the media. Need I say that derelict journalists are often an essential accessory to the tyrannical state. Many were executed right along with Nazi officers at the Nuremberg tribunal. Most of the corporate media have been derelict since long before Trump took office, and this is clear to us antiauthritarians and nonpartisans who can look at current events with some degree of objectivity.

It is hard to take seriously a scholar who so grossly misjudged recent history and peppered a work on such an important topic with absurdity.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on September 8, 2020
Review Body:
It looked like just my kind of read: The excerpts from journalist's reviews and 6,000+ Amazon readers fired my interest, but a quick browse with the "Look Inside" option quickly deflated my enthusiasm.

The fuzzy intellectual rigor which seems to conflate elections with democracy, and oppression only with totalitarian regimes leaves a huge undefined gap between his concepts. Analogous to tribal languages which only count "one, two and "many", except that Mr. Snyder sees nations as democracies, oligarchies, and dictatorships, apparently combining the last two.

His approval of the American founding fathers' system of constitutional checks & balances is a bit selective and quite outdated. Many--if not most--of those checks have been gradually flattened by the metastasis of government, abetted by Supreme Court justices committed to an "evolutionary" vision of the constitution. Snyder doesn't seem to have noticed the vast bureaucracies that have absorbed our former liberties, perhaps because we still have elections.

Our founders were well ahead of Lord Acton in perceiving that inevitable corruption that attends increases in power, and they aimed (not quite successfully) to severely limit federal powers. By contrast Snyder celebrates Britain's post-war "democratic moments" in which the Labour Party triumphed and vastly expanded government supervision of British life.

Defending democratic institutions seems unassailable advice. He says, "So choose an institution you care about--a court, a newspaper, a law, a labor union--and take its side." But he offers no advice for evaluating these choices--Just do it. This seems like an invitation to join a tribe, pin on a virtue badge and take to the streets or an editorial page, submerging your reason in the flow of mass movement. No suggested evaluation of the consequences should your chosen cause succeed.

This is how the Fascist movements he deplores start: Popular moral dogmas, slogans, raised fists, dehumanized adversaries. "Caring" won't prevent this. At minimum, a balanced historical perspective, critical evaluation, and respect for others' rights are needed.

I am surely oversimplifying the thoughts of this prolific Yale professor, but his choice of words, omissions, and murky generalizations in this brief sample suggest I won't learn much by reading the whole 128 pages.

Review Body:
Be warned: this book is not what you are led to believe by the title. I picked this up in hopes of a book that would thoughtfully apply historical lessons of tyranny to our time, a topic of that could and should be bipartisan. However, what I got was the standard "Trump is bad, he's the next Hitler." just wrapped in the air of academic superiority you would expect from a Yale professor. This is nothing more than the tripe you would get from a Rachel Maddow or Lawrence O'Donnell just wrapped in a more academic tone.

The book could be good IF Snyder had applied lessons from the past equally - and yes they can apply to both sides - to both sides of the American political divide. Unfortunately, like most on the modern left, he starts with the aforementioned premise of Trump as another Hitler than proceeds to try and shape these lessons to his premise.

I do not have blind allegiance to Trump as some do. He is wrong on many things and some of Snyder's points about him are valid. However, some of these same lessons could just as easily be applied to Democrats. For example, in his chapter on terror management, he rightly notes how politicians could use fear of terrorism to push anti-freedom measures that grow government power. However, he completely ignores one of the most contemporary uses of this tactic that comes from the left: immediately pouncing on any shooting to attack our fundamental right to bear arms. Not a single word devoted to this, which evidences Snyder's bias.

In a passage on the trade off between freedom and security, he notes that government's job is to make us more free and more secure. This cannot possibly be true and a Yale historian should better understand this than someone with non-Ivy engineering and finance degrees. Government CANNOT make us more free because government, by definition, is a limit on freedom. Our most free state is anarchy. Government is instituted to bring order to society and naturally to limit the rawest of freedom.

Snyder notes that for young people to make history they will need to now it. That is very true and that includes a full understanding of liberty as established by our Founding Fathers, not an agenda-driven application of history's worst tyrants, i.e. Hitler and Stalin, to a flawed President that in no objective manner resembles the monsters of the mid-2oth century.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 20, 2020
Review Body:
I listened to this book on the Overdrive library app, and consider it a classic example of what could be a good book but with some very poor application. First, to give the author credit where it is due: I largely agree with most of the general arguments he makes, and these are points worth considering. I will say that much of the analysis is somewhat superficial and could be developed a lot more, although this is a short book so I can forgive that. I actually kind of liked the book at first, but as you go it through the author gets more and more into his application to modern American politics, and here is where my primary criticism is. The author discredits himself to a large extent with a very obvious bias regarding current American politics. Not that all of his application is wrong, but he shows a willingness to completely trust certain sources of information because of pre-existing political loyalties. One of the main points he makes is that we have to investigate what we hear or read, but a question he fails to address is "How"? Do you investigate what you read by going to your favorite news source or a "fact check" type of site? The point is that true investigation is much more than that, and I think here is one point where the author fails the reader.
I won't say that the author's application to American politics is 100% wrong or anything, but it is very myopic and one sided, as well as based on some very dubious information. Politically speaking, he certainly fails to look both ways before crossing the street.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 20, 2018
Review Body:
Writing in 2017, the author of this book says at one point, "We can be sure that the elections of 2018, assuming they take place...'

Do you need to know anything else about the political one-sidedness the author brings to this book? He seems to have a mild case of Trump Delusion Syndrome.

If you pick a copy of this book up in your local bookstore, as I did, you might make the same mistake that I did. The author is a well-credentialed professor of history, you would think. The "twenty lessons" format in a little book like this promises a bit of distilled and penetrating thought on each point, you would think.

But you would be wrong. To the extent that the author describes 20th European history, his coverage is necessarily superficial and certainly not wrong. However, it is incomplete. He manages to bring up "right wing" totalitarians, Hitler and Putin, without mentioning "left wing" totalitarians, Lenin and Stalin (although he does mention Polish resistance to communism). He comes to the defense of the main stream media, without seeming to have any notion of the extent to which political opinions of the journalists all sides infect their reporting.

So, if your politics leans left, this book will not do much more than affirm you in your opinions, whereas if they lean right, you will not find any deeply reasoned arguments to challenge your viewpoint.

Don't waste your money, either way. I tossed my copy in the recycle bin, but on reflection am going to put it in a nearby Little Free Library, so someone else won't waste theirs.

One Star because that's where I have to start, plus one Star because the historical information might be useful for someone who has forgotten their 9th grade world history class.

The book is, in fact, a quickly written sermon with surprisingly little historical content. Yes, we find a bit of Hitler, Stalin, Putin, Havel. But of course it is really a book about Trump and about Hillary. For each "lesson," the reader gets a few paragraphs that are more stream-of-consciousness than anything else.

There is simply very little here in the way of stimulating analysis -- if you truly want that, check out Gore Vidal's work. But if you are looking for a trite little book with colorless language that nevertheless delivers your daily serving of red meat, then this book should do nicely.

Review Body: The book has interesting observations and is worth a read. However, the author is very partisan, and has a variety of criticisms of President Trump. Using Trump as an example of "tyranny" betrays any sense of impartiality the reader might have hoped to find. Snyder, in describing Trump in various ways, is blind to the fact that he could have described both Hillary and Obama in the same way. The arguably tyrannical (certainly autocratic) executive orders of Obama that may have exceeded his constitutional authority and Hillary's describing half the nation as "deplorables" are just two examples. The author is also ignorant of economics, citing Trump's claim of cutting taxes and reducing national debt as contradictory and amounting to "magical thinking." In fact, taxes have been cut, hundreds of companies (~200 at last count) have lauded the move and passed money on to employees, and billions of dollars have flowed back to America from overseas. What Snyder saw, in his partisan myopia, as flawed thinking was in fact sound economic theory--although not a theory everyone agrees with. Snyder, quick to point out his perceived Trumpian flaws, is curiously silent on the tyranny of Democrat policy on race, taxation, over-regulation, federal control, language redefinition, and so on. Snyder was nimble in labeling Trump's use of language as a form of tyranny, but absolutely club-footed in turning to the humiliations of the English language used by the left--some would say regressive left--on redefining hate, phobia, free speech, and even pronouns in an effort to engineer our worldview into a leftist vision. Snyder thus fails to follow the good advice of his own book by going along with the Trump-bashing hyperbole that has gripped the nation while ignoring even more lamentable behavior from elsewhere on the political spectrum. Far from standing out from the crowd, Snyder joined it with gusto.

Potential readers would be far better served by reading Hayek’s "Road to Serfdom" or one of Milton Friedman’s several books on the subject instead.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on June 23, 2017
Review Body:
Before even opening the page, I made a prediction to myself about ON TYRANNY. It would be good in a particular way and bad in a particular way. Maybe I am a psychic. Right on both counts.

The good? After describing tyranny (“usurpation of power by a single individual or group, or the circumvention of law by rulers for their own benefit”) Timothy Snyder serves up often very good short essays on issues large and small to stop the advance of it. Contained within these little essays are many gems, such as that it is a mistake to think that those who rose to power through certain institutions cannot change or destroy those institutions.

The bad, however, was foreseeable a mile away. Right near the get go, we know where it is heading with the assertion that “[b]oth fascism and communism were responses to globalization.” Really? It seems more likely that with INTERNATIONAL socialism calling for the workers of the THE WORLD to unite, Snyder might be off target. And his use of the word ‘globalization’ is a clear indicator that he intends to augment his timeless lessons and historical examples with current examples in our modern day, but, and you know it is coming, current examples in only one direction.

Let me just say that, my predictive powers are fully operational.

Snyder includes so many partisan examples, and misses so many others outside of his obvious political leanings, that a complete response is not possible other than through a whole new book. Still, a few examples may be useful.

In a real chortler, in the chapter on being wary of paramilitaries, Snyder warns of violent right-wing groups, and Trump wanting to use a private security force. One can tell how disconnected another is from reality when, despite current and historical political violence originating overwhelmingly on the Left, they either blame the Right for its (significantly less) violent tendencies or, pathetically, try to split the difference. Which side is Antifa from? SDS? The Weathermen? How many Hillary Clinton supporters were assaulted on the street? Please, Snyder, spare me.

Snyder accuses Trump of using language that rejects legitimate opposition. Yet as far back as I can remember (and I am in my 50s), the Left has used words such as racist or fascist so consistently and incessantly to describe mainstream conservative views that an anthropologist from Mars could be forgiven for believing that the words ‘conservative’ and ‘racist’ (or ‘fascist’) were interchangeable.

In the chapter Believe in truth, Snyder warns against shamanistic incantation in our language. Like elevating the word ‘diversity’ to as commonly used as the word ‘the’? No, no, of course not. Like Trump calling his opponent Crooked Hillary. Despite the rough and tumble that accompanies politics, everyone can see how that just goes all out of bounds, and is meant to take us to the world of ‘magical thinking’ (an actual phrase Snyder discusses in this same chapter). And although our last president made a TV journalist experience a thrill up his leg, was referred to as a ‘Lightworker’ by a columnist in a major daily newspaper, and himself said that his election would be the moment when the rise of the oceans would begin to slow and the Earth would begin to heal, Snyder takes no notice. Maybe he was absent those days.

If there were any doubt about Snyder’s credibility, he throws it away in Chapter 19 (Be a patriot), when he states that “[i]t is not patriotic to call upon Russia to intervene in an American presidential election.” That certainly is a true statement when viewed in isolation. But let us not kid ourselves, it was not made in isolation. At this point in the book (page 112 of 126), this was a dig at Trump channeling months of bombastic accusations and zero evidence.

In a final example of Snyder using very legitimate concepts discussed in this book for purely partisan ends, he reminds us that Trump’s phrase “America First” was used by a committee trying to prevent the U.S. from opposing Nazi Germany. Yeah, and Obama’s “Forward” was as Marxist as it comes. One might argue that, as Trump is now president, he is the legitimate target. But Snyder provides us with numerous other historical examples, amazingly stopping at the rise of modern liberalism outside the Soviet sphere and jumping right to Trump instead, time after time after time.

Given the importance of the messages in ON TYRANNY, their spoliation for current political points is rather sad. It is, however, not unexpected.

I bought/read this after hearing a mediocre interview of the author on the Sam Harris podcast. I was hoping the book would somehow be better, but knew it would at least be short.

It was generic leftist "the sky is falling" ranting. There is an attempt to make it seem like there are some real fundamental truths about defending a democratic society against threats like nazism or communism, but it was really just "be a good leftist", "pay the (print) news media", etc. Skip.

Review Body: I found this book to be disappointingly self-evident. It was clearly written in haste, in response to the recent election. I wish the author used a wider range of historical sources rather than drawing inexact parallels with the Nazi era, especially since his other book (Black Earth) is so meticulous in its discussion of the Holocaust.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on June 5, 2017
Review Body: The author spoke on Sam Harris podcast, so I purchased this text. It is, trite, and full of platitudes and aphorisms. Tim Snyder does go into details and provide some insights and explanations into why the platitudes (lessons/rules) are given, however, even though the historical events are contextualized towards the lessons, they 'beware' tone is written like a children's spooky book, such as Goosebumps. Make sense? It's just not a very valuable read. It would be better to read historical text and draw your own conclusions and contextual 'lessons'.
